property_summary: After any call to transferOwnership, the owner must be set to the supplied newOwner parameter; the bug sets owner to msg.sender instead, violating this for any caller other than newOwner.

After a successful transferOwnership call by the current owner, the owner must remain the caller's address; the bug sets owner to msg.sender regardless, so a subsequent call by the new owner (who is not the original owner) would fail the onlyOwner check, violating the invariant that ownership actually transfers.
After the current owner calls transferOwnership with a newOwner, the correctly transferred owner must match newOwner; the bug sets owner to msg.sender, breaking this for any newOwner != msg.sender.

After a successful transferOwnership call by the owner, the new owner (the caller) must be able to call a function restricted by onlyOwner; the bug sets owner to the original owner (msg.sender) instead of the new owner, so the new owner cannot pass the onlyOwner check.

After a successful transferOwnership call from the current owner, a subsequent call to transferOwnership by the previous owner (now no longer the owner) must revert; the bug leaves the caller as owner, so their subsequent call succeeds.
After any call to transferOwnership with a valid new owner, the owner must equal the new owner; the mutant sets owner to address(0) instead, breaking this invariant.

For any caller that is the current owner, after transferOwnership(x) succeeds, owner must equal the arg x passed in; the mutant always sets owner to address(0), so it differs whenever x != address(0).
After transferOwnership is called by the owner, the owner state variable should be updated to the new owner; the buggy version leaves owner unchanged.

For any initial owner and any new owner, after the current owner calls transferOwnership, the owner variable must equal the newOwner argument; the buggy version fails this because it never assigns the new address.

For any owner and any new owner, after a call to transferOwnership, the owner remains the original owner; the buggy mutant fails because it never updates owner, so after the call the owner still equals the original owner.
After the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner), the owner must equal newOwner; the mutant never updates owner so it stays unchanged.
After the current owner calls transferOwnership(newOwner), the owner() must equal newOwner; the buggy version never assigns newOwner so owner() stays unchanged.
transferOwnership must succeed for the current owner, but the buggy modifier causes it to always revert.
For any caller that is the current owner, a transferOwnership call to a non-zero new owner should succeed (not revert); the buggy version always reverts due to the meaningless require(false).

For any caller, if a transferOwnership call does not revert, the owner must be updated to newOwner; the buggy modifier (require(false)) makes it always revert, but the reference can succeed for the current owner.
For any caller and any new owner, if the caller is the current owner, transferOwnership succeeds and sets owner to the new owner; the buggy version always reverts, so no new owner is set.
For any caller, a call to owned() must not revert; the buggy modifier requires false, making owned() always revert.

For any caller who is the owner, a call to owned() must succeed and not revert. The reference satisfies this by requiring msg.sender == owner, while the buggy version always reverts regardless of caller.

A non-zero-callvalue call to owned should always revert, but after a revert the owner of contract C must remain unchanged; the buggy contract satisfies the revert but fails to preserve the owner invariant when the call is made with value.

For any owner and any caller, after a call to owned() the owner must remain unchanged; the buggy contract's always-reverting modifier still leaves owner untouched, but the previous attempts failed to find a distinguishing input because the invariant holds for both. Widening the domain to include the initial owner as a fuzzed parameter and asserting that the owner after calling owned() equals the original owner passes on the reference for all inputs and fails on the mutant when a non-zero-callvalue call is made by the owner, causing the mutant's always-reverting transferOwnership to be uncallable and thus the owner remains unchanged—however the real difference is that in the reference, only the owner can call owned() without revert, so we assert that for the owner caller, owned() does not revert; the mutant always reverts, breaking the rule.
